newsitem.title: PAPUA NEW GUINEA: Tension mounts in Papua New Guinea crisis.
newsitem.headline: Tension mounts in Papua New Guinea crisis.

text.p: Tensions mounted in Papua New Guinea on Thursday as protesters and soldiers demanded the reinstatement of a sacked army chief and criminal gangs took advantage of a political crisis to go on the rampage.
Police fired tear gas against looters around the city and shots rang out through the day near an army barracks where thousands of people gathered to protest against Prime Minister Sir Julius Chan.
Confrontation between police and troops was narrowly avoided after running battles between police and protestors spilled into the sprawling Murray barracks.

Scores of protesters ran in through the barracks gate and police fired tear gas into the compound after them, angering soldiers who have remained inside the barracks since the crisis erupted on Monday.
A group of enraged soldiers started kicking down the door of the armoury for weapons but were stopped by junior officers who had to draw their own sidearms.
The officers quickly managed to calm down the situation.
While the army has been the focus for protests against Chan, the police force is believed to be backing the government.
Any confrontation between the forces, traditional rivals, would have unpredictable consequences for democracy in the troubled South Pacific nation.

The crisis began on Monday when Brigadier-General Jerry Singirok demanded that Chan resign for hiring foreign mercenaries to end a conflict on Bougainville island where secessionist rebels have been battling the government since 1988. Chan promptly sacked his army commander.

Thursday's unrest initially appeared to be more criminal than political. Local gangs known as "rascals" make Port Moresby one of the world's most dangerous places even in normal times and looters roamed the run-down city of around 150,000 people.
Schools, banks and many businesses were closed and police erected roadblocks on major roads.
Army officers gave a defence ministry official a petition with 4,700 signatures -- representing virtually all army personnel -- demanding that Singirok be reinstated.

The petition demanded that all those connected with the mercenary operation stand down and an independent inquiry be set up to investigate the US$28 million contract with British military company Sandline International.
But as a deadline set by the petition passed, Singirok himself told reporters that he would accept his sacking as long as it proved legal and constitutional.
With gunfire echoing on the streets outside, Singirok gave a news conference in the garden of his residence in the barracks, looking relaxed in a sports shirt and playing with a pet dog.
"What is happening out here on the streets and around the country is the cries of millions of Papua New Guineans who do not have (basic) services," the 40-year-old general said.
"I am no longer the commander. I have no jurisdiction over soldiers or civilians. I have continually appealed to the men to be loyal to the defence force," he added.
"I think it is a political situation now -- the politicians need to come out now and talk to the people."

Prime Minister Chan signalled a climbdown over the mercenaries on Wednesday. By that time the first six of 40 mercenaries, who are mostly South African, had left the South Pacific nation saying the contract was already terminated.

Chan has said Singirok helped negotiate the mercenary deal and supported it, but Singirok said on Thursday he began his revolt because the mercenaries were about to launch a "military onslaught" on the copper-rich island Bougainville.
"I would have had to tell the international community and the people of the region why I used such force against civilian targets and rebel targets," the general said.

He refuted declarations by Chan that the mercenaries, mostly South African veterans, would only have been used for training, saying they would have been active on the front lines against Bougainville's ragtag rebel guerrillas.

Army officers said a further six mercenaries left Papua New Guinea on Thursday, leaving 55 behind. One officer said there had originally been nearly 70 mercenaries in the country rather than 40 acknowledged by the government.
